segment:
Mara stepped out onto the concrete of the wide porch and let him lead her down the stairs.

“You look so different when you’re tired.”

Mara looked up at his side profile, surprised to see him watching her face. “Is that bad?”

“No, I like it. It’s like you’re a little younger.”

“I didn’t think I could get much younger.” She made herself say that as lightly as he’d said the first thing.

He smiled without turning toward her and kept his voice matter-of-fact. “You don’t look tired. You look thoughtful.” He looked over at her, a brief half glance that seemed to say “I like you here with me.”

“My eyes just feel heavy.” She was getting used to feeling his fingers close around hers, steady and firm but not squeezing. It kept her from feeling how heavy her legs felt walking on the black asphalt of the parking lot.

He nodded slightly. “Your forehead’s creased, but they don’t look red and irritated like sometimes.”

Mara’s eyebrows went up a fraction and she gave him an odd look. She didn’t want to know how her eyes looked.

“That’s not what I meant,” he said, noticing the way her eyes went big and startled for just a second. “You can drop the guard. That was your problem.” He meant something other than eyes, something like her muscles, her breathing, her whole body.

He didn’t say anything else as they walked together in the dark toward the city and the lights of the bay. She made herself look up at the sky with his eyes and breathe as slowly and easily as him. They were both in sneakers, walking without touching except where their fingers held each other. The warm night air smelled like a hot metal roof and flowers from an open window.

“You said I could ask anything.”

“Yeah?” He tilted his head toward hers. “What is it?”

She looked down at the black pavement under her feet and tried to get her breathing to stay slow and easy. Her skin felt tight around her bones.

“Would you help me if I asked?”

He nodded slowly. “Yeah.”

“I think I might want to ask for something.” Her voice was a little shaky.

“That’s good,” he said. His eyes stayed on her face and his right arm kept her steady. His voice stayed low and calm even though she could feel his muscles tightening with tension. She was so tired she felt like she’d been running for hours without stopping. Her hands were trembling and the sweat on her back felt cold in the breeze.

“What would you want me to do?”

“Just hold me.”

segment:
“It’s cool in the woods,” Jonah said. “The wind makes it feel colder. Do you have a coat?”

“No.”

“I’ll carry your bag.” Mara carried nothing, but she’d told him so twice in two weeks. “Hold on to me when you need to, okay?”

The hand he held still felt light, barely touching her. Mara looked at their joined wrists and elbows before looking into his face again.

“Will you be here tomorrow?”

“I don’t think so,” Jonah said. “My schedule’s full.”

Mara looked at the hand on his belt buckle and waited.

She saw him notice. His eyes went to her elbow, then back to her face. “Do you want to tell me something?”

She didn’t. Mara looked down again, saw their wrists linked by a single strip of leather. “If you put your hand there—” She pointed to the gap between her elbow and his— “my hand will have somewhere to go.”

Jonah bent and waited.

She slid her fingers through the strip and felt her arm against his shoulder. Her hair smelled like the cool, dry air they’d just left.

He’d stopped smiling but his shoulders stayed back. Mara set her cheek on his shoulder and tilted her head so that his eyes and hers met in the mirror.

“I’m scared.” She let his shirt and shoulder hide her tears. He turned and held her in one arm, her bag in the other, and she felt warm skin on her cheek. “It’s dark,” Mara said. “I like holding on to you.”

“Okay,” Jonah said into her hair. “How do you want to go home?”

He meant which way, but Mara had no idea. She said, “I don’t know,” and let her tears run.

Jonah touched her with his palm just below her ear, held her there until she stopped. “You look like you’re asleep.”

“I’m not.”

“I know.” The hand didn’t move until Mara did, then came down to her shoulder and rested there. Mara tilted her face into his hand, felt the skin there cool and soft. He lifted her up from his shoulder, turned their joined hands to rest her on his arm, and held her there without touching her wrist or elbow.

“Should we stay here?” Jonah asked.

“No,” Mara said. “I want to go home.”

He didn’t look down as they walked through a cold, still night. His eyes went up into the trees until the wind changed the smell and touched his cheek. Then he looked past her and kept looking in that direction as if it were the only one.

When their shoulders and arms met in the same way Mara knew how his body felt from every side. If he kept looking somewhere else they might have nothing left to say, but if he didn’t look she’d never know where they were going.

Mara turned her face into the wind. Her skin still smelled like him.

“I don’t see anything,” Mara said. “Do you?”

segment:
“Tell me what we did,” Jonah said after a moment. “I couldn’t keep track of you.”

She told him. He made a small surprised noise when she described the touch with the stranger and frowned when she described leaving the group. Mara finished and they were quiet for a few breaths.

“I can tell you about my side if you want to hear.” Jonah paused again, eyes on hers, his breath audible in the night air. “Do you want to hear?”

“Sure,” she said. She cleared her throat because it was tight with the strain of listening closely for any sign that he didn’t want to talk about himself.

He spoke and she felt that her left hand wasn’t in the right place. She couldn’t focus on his voice if her eyes were on their hands and she could tell if her eyes weren’t on their hands because his left thumb moved under hers when he paused between sentences. She knew that if she could keep still for long enough it would make sense to her.

“That’s what we did, anyway,” Jonah said, closing one hand on her arm just above the elbow and watching her eyes. The pressure was light, almost absent—less than a caress and more than a touch of reassurance. He was waiting to see if she moved or stepped away.

Mara had the idea of pulling her arm free so she could turn and face him. Then his face was too much to manage and she knew that the arm would make sense if she kept still for long enough. His pressure hadn’t changed but it didn’t stop being there either.

“I’m sorry about your session,” she said after a few breaths. Jonah’s face shifted as if he were about to speak. Instead he smiled and held still without looking away. Mara’s lips moved with the idea of kissing him but stopped before his face was close enough.

“I want to kiss you,” Jonah said when the air became too dry to bear any longer.

“Okay.” She shifted her weight to her left foot and felt the muscles in their arms stretch without touching.

Jonah shifted to a hip angle and looked at her lips instead of her eyes. Mara held still until she felt that moving would make sense. Her face turned toward his shoulder as her feet made her turn toward his left side. Jonah’s breath changed to a deep, calm pattern without sound, so calm it might have been apnea.

Then they touched and the rest was a series of movements so small she could only tell which happened first by remembering what it felt like.

segment:
Their joined hands hung between them. She wasn’t sure where to put hers when he spoke, still watching her.

“Did you need me to go home with you?” He turned his palm up and tucked her fingers closer into his. “I’m okay either way.”

She knew what he was asking. She nodded without looking at his mouth. “I just need to talk for a while.” She knew that too: words wouldn’t change her feelings. They weren’t supposed to.

His hand stayed in hers when they left the porch and turned into the street. The light from the Institute front steps fell on a redbrick path. The scent of jasmine thickened the air.

A breeze brushed her face. She looked up for stars through the high eucalyptus, but she couldn’t see through the tree canopy. She could hear night birds, owls mostly, but no crickets or other insects.

She didn’t know how long they stood, waiting. Her left foot ached as if it had been asleep but the rest of her was awake. Jonah didn’t say “Let’s go” or “Wait” or “Where do you want to walk?” When she turned he stepped forward with her.

They walked without talking, the only sounds their feet and their breath. She didn’t look at him except to feel him moving beside her. They passed a small house with a dark window above the front steps. Then the next one and the next, then no more houses. When they passed the first dark trees she felt the night close in.

The pavement ended where two driveways had met. They could have been on a dirt road, but there weren’t any streetlights or other cars. It was dark enough for her to see his face without him turning toward her.

She wasn’t sure when they stopped walking. She might have stopped moving first, but he didn’t ask if she had meant it. When he put his hand on the small of her back it was just there, a little pressure that wouldn’t move her or let her stumble.

His lips touched the corner of her mouth when she turned toward him and his left hand slid to her neck. His mouth moved over hers once, twice, three times as if he didn’t know what she would do next. She turned more deeply into him when he put his right hand under her chin to rest with hers. He didn’t break the kiss; she lifted her hand to let it rest where it wanted to be, on his jaw and the curve of his neck. When her fingers touched his hair his whole body sighed out a long breath and he cupped the back of her neck.

“That was a scary thing to do.” His lips brushed the corner of her mouth. “I’m glad I did it.”

segment:
He walked down the steps at her pace without touching her. As they walked he fell in a quarter turn ahead so her left arm brushed the back of his hand every two or three steps. When he reached for her shoulder on a hill she moved into the pressure to show him her weight was on its way. He walked as if he didn’t need to know when she’d get there—as if he knew it already.

Her shoe stepped in a soft spot of mud; Jonah stopped in front of her and put his left hand near her face, palm down. He balanced her on the inside of her forearm with just enough pressure to keep her from falling but not enough to make her stumble.

“Careful,” he said.

She set her left hand on his forearm and used his arm for balance, letting him guide her forward with his thumb as she lifted her foot out of the mud. He let her test the ground around his shoe before moving his own foot, so they never stood on mud at the same time.

The path widened, but he didn’t let go; as her hand stayed on his forearm he moved it down to his upper arm in one fluid motion, then back to his forearm after three steps, like a silent exchange. Mara felt a pull in her throat and stopped walking.

“Can I do this?” she asked, and wrapped the other arm around the forearm she’d just let go.

She heard a deep inhale and held her breath. After a slow second she felt his arms come up around her waist without releasing her forearm—almost a cradle, but not quite. Her shoulder rested under his chin. His lips were cool on the top of her head.

He didn’t answer, so she spoke again. “Can I?”

“You’ve already asked twice,” he said in an easy voice, and dropped his arms without saying yes or no.

His steps stayed sure as if the night wasn’t dark at all. Mara had to look ahead of her feet to avoid a rut in the road, but Jonah stepped past it as if he could see it by touch alone.

When the road flattened out into an asphalt shoulder Mara stopped walking. “I don’t need to hold on now.”

“You still have my arm,” Jonah said without stopping.

“Not now.” Mara let go and felt her breathing deepen. “Now I’m okay.”

“Okay?”

“To walk alone.” She looked straight ahead, wishing she had the words for what was in her mind.

His steps slowed to a stop. She heard him inhale without saying anything—not for breath but for time. His throat worked as he swallowed. Then he walked ahead, slowly. “I could walk beside you,” he said.
